To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
extinction risk assessment methods are available for marine species, and that these methods should be used to assess extinction risk of marine species.

extinction risk can be assessed by: (i) comparing life-history traits of marine fish species with those of terrestrial species that are known to have gone extinct; (ii) using the rate of change of abundance of a population as an indicator of extinction risk; (iii) comparing the current population size of a species to its maximum historical size; or (iv) using demographic methods to assess the risk that the population size will decline below some critical threshold.

there is no single method for assessing extinction risk, but there are a number of useful methods that are well suited to different types of data and different types of species.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the methods for assessing extinction risk are well developed for species with high levels of fishing pressure and/or low productivity, but are much less well developed for species that exhibit narrow geographical distributions and/or ecological specialization.
the methods used for assessing risk of extinction in fishes are not well developed, particularly for species with narrow geographical ranges or ecological specialization.
extinction risk assessment for marine fishes is a complex process that is best approached in stages and with a clear understanding of the limitations and assumptions of the methods used.
